target: Nous avons des voisins sympas.
english: We have nice neighbors.
old: Adjectives agree in gender and number. 'Sympa' is invariable informally, but standard form: sympathique/sympathiques.
focus: Keep the register point that sympa is the casual clip of sympathique; drop the invariability claim, which the card's own 'sympas' contradicts.

target: Les chaussures marron sont jolies.
english: The brown shoes are pretty.
old: Some color adjectives are invariable (never change form): marron, orange, rose (when used for specific shades). Exception: rose does agree.
focus: Marron never agrees, which is why 'les chaussures marron' has no -s; cut the self-contradicting rose/orange tangent.

target: Le jardin de mon voisin est joli.
english: My neighbor's garden is pretty.
old: Possession uses 'de': le livre de Marie (Marie's book), la voiture de mon père (my father's car). No apostrophe-s in French.
focus: Keep the no-apostrophe-s contrast but anchor the worked example in this card's own 'le jardin de mon voisin' instead of sibling-only examples.

target: Il fait froid dehors.
english: It's cold outside.
old: Wrong: `il est froid` would mean 'he is cold' (about a person). For weather, always `il fait`.
focus: Excellent il-fait-not-il-est weather trap; strip the backticks and keep the wrong-vs-right contrast anchored to 'il fait froid'.

target: Ça te plaît ici ?
english: Do you like it here?
old: Three question forms: intonation ('Tu viens?'), 'est-ce que', or inversion ('Viens-tu?').
focus: Anchor to THIS card: an intonation question keeps statement word order plus rising tone, the default in speech – quote 'Ca te plait ici ?' and drop the off-card est-ce que/inversion examples.

target: Elle est brune aux yeux verts.
english: She is brunette with green eyes.
old: 'Brun/brune' changes form for gender. 'Vert/verte' also changes. The final consonant is pronounced in feminine.
focus: One rule: the feminine ending makes the silent final consonant audible – brun ends silent, brune sounds the n. Quote 'brune' from this card; cut the second vert/verte rule.

target: Elle est petite et mince.
english: She is short and slim.
old: Adjectives agree in gender: petit/petite, mince stays the same (ends in -e already). Two adjectives joined by 'et'.
focus: petite shows feminine agreement (petit/petite); cut the 'two adjectives joined by et' filler – one rule only

target: Vingt et un, trente, quarante, cinquante.
english: Twenty-one, thirty, forty, fifty.
old: Numbers 21-69 follow a pattern: vingt et un (21), trente-deux (32). After 70, French uses base-20: soixante-dix (70), quatre-vingts (80).
focus: vingt et un takes 'et' for 21 (also 31, 41…); drop the 70+/base-20 preview – fr-0906 already covers it

target: Elle est fière de son travail.
english: She is proud of her work.
old: 'Fier' (m.) → 'fière' (f.) = proud. The accent changes: fier/fière. 'Fier de' = proud of.
focus: fier gains a grave accent in the feminine – fière, like premier/première; cut the 'fier de = proud of' gloss

target: Il est sorti acheter du pain.
english: He went out to buy bread.
old: Sortir uses être when intransitive: il est sorti.
focus: sortir takes être not avoir – 'il est sorti'; say it in plain words, not 'intransitive'

target: Nous sommes restés à l'hôtel ce jour-là.
english: We stayed at the hotel that day.
old: Rester uses être. Masculine plural subject: restes.
focus: rester takes être even though nothing moves – the edge case; fix the wrong example 'restes' to 'restés' (agrees with nous)

target: Regarde le beau coucher de soleil sur la mer.
english: Look at the beautiful sunset over the sea.
old: 'Regarde' is the tu-form imperative. 'Regardez' for vous-form. Both can be used to draw attention.
focus: tu-imperative drops the -s: tu regardes but 'Regarde !' – that trap, not the tu/vous form list

target: Je me lève à sept heures.
english: I get up at seven o'clock.
old: Reflexive verbs use reflexive pronouns: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève, nous nous levons. The pronoun matches the subject.
focus: French says 'I raise myself' – 'je me lève'; the pronoun is mandatory. Cut the tu/il/nous paradigm list

target: J'ai mangé au restaurant hier soir.
english: I ate at the restaurant last night.
old: 'Au restaurant' uses 'au' (à + le). Time markers like 'hier soir' confirm passé composé.
focus: au = à + le, mandatory contraction ('au restaurant'); drop the time-marker second rule

target: Je préparais toujours le thé à cinq heures de l'après-midi.
english: I always used to make tea at five in the afternoon.
old: le / la → l' before a vowel: l'homme, l'eau. Possessives flip too: ma → mon before a vowel, so "mon amie" even though amie is feminine.
focus: elision is in the card: l'après-midi (le → l' before a vowel); quote it and drop the ma/mon amie second rule

target: Tu connaissais déjà la réponse quand le professeur a posé la question ?
english: Did you already know the answer when the teacher asked the question?
old: 'Toujours' or 'souvent' in past context → imparfait (habitual). 'Un jour' or 'soudain' → passé composé (specific event).
focus: the card itself contrasts connaissais (ongoing state) with a posé (one event) – anchor there; the toujours/soudain signal words aren't in this sentence

target: Nous sommes lundi.
english: It's Monday.
old: Days of the week: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. No capitals. 'Le lundi' = on Mondays (habitual).
focus: 'Nous sommes lundi' – French says 'we are Monday' for dates; keep the no-capitals nugget, cut the seven-day vocab list

target: Je vais bientôt partir.
english: I'm going to leave soon.
old: Near future: aller + infinitive. Je vais manger = I'm going to eat. Very common at A1, often preferred over future tense.
focus: aller + infinitive = going-to future, anchored in 'je vais bientôt partir'; cut the 'very common at A1' meta-commentary

target: Il y a du soleil.
english: It's sunny.
old: Don't confuse `il y a` (there is) with `il a` (he has) or `il a y` (doesn't exist). The `y` is mandatory.
focus: il y a vs il a confusable pair, anchored in 'il y a du soleil'; strip the backticks and cut the "il a y (doesn't exist)" filler

target: Nous sommes le quinze mars.
english: It's March fifteenth.
old: Dates: le + number + month. 'Le premier' for the 1st, then cardinal numbers: le deux, le trois. Months are lowercase.
focus: dates use plain numbers – 'le quinze mars' where English says 'fifteenth'; only le premier is ordinal. Quote the card's quinze

target: En fait, je préfère rester ici.
english: Actually, I prefer to stay here.
old: 'En fait' = actually / in fact. Very useful connector for correcting or clarifying what you just said.
focus: Anchor 'En fait' as the real word for 'actually' – the false friend 'actuellement' means 'currently'; cut the 'very useful connector' filler.

target: Ils dinaient au restaurant quand la lumière s'est eteinte.
english: They were having dinner at the restaurant when the light went out.
old: Dining (ongoing activity) vs lights going out (sudden event). The tense contrast tells the story.
focus: Good ongoing-vs-sudden insight but it never quotes the French – anchor on 'dinaient' (ongoing backdrop) vs 's'est éteinte' (the interrupting event).

target: Je voulais acheter un gâteau mais la boulangerie a fermé.
english: I wanted to buy a cake but the bakery closed.
old: Voulais (imparfait) = ongoing desire. A ferme (PC) = completed event that changed things.
focus: Keep the voulais = ongoing want vs a fermé = event-that-ended-it contrast; fix the missing accent ('a fermé', not 'A ferme') and spell out passé composé instead of 'PC'.

target: Elle est montée au troisième étage.
english: She went up to the third floor.
old: With `être`, agreement matters: a woman writes `je suis allée`, men `je suis allé`. Plural feminine `nous sommes allées`. Sounds the same; spelling changes.
focus: Strip the backticks and anchor on this card's 'est montée' – keep the strong hook that être-agreement changes spelling only, the ending is silent in speech.

target: Il a été malade pendant une semaine.
english: He was sick for a week.
old: 'Être' → 'été'. The past participle is invariable: il a été, elle a été (no agreement with 'avoir').
focus: Lead with the real surprise: être's own passé composé takes avoir – 'il a été', never 'il est été'; drop the invariable-participle aside.

target: Tu as fait attention en traversant la rue ?
english: Did you pay attention while crossing the street?
old: Faire attention = to pay attention or to be careful. Past participle: fait.
focus: One rule only: French 'makes' attention – 'faire attention' = pay attention / be careful; cut the tacked-on participle note.

target: Il y avait toujours du monde dans ce restaurant.
english: There were always people in this restaurant.
old: `y` = 'there' or 'to it' – replaces a place or `à + thing`. `Tu vas au cinéma? Oui, j'y vais` (Yes, I'm going there). Saves you repeating the location.
focus: Retarget to this card's fixed expression: 'il y avait' = 'there was/were', the past of 'il y a'; strip backticks and drop the j'y vais examples that aren't this usage.

target: Nous sommes passés par le centre-ville.
english: We went through the city center.
old: Passer uses être when meaning to pass by or through (intransitive).
focus: Drop the 'intransitive' jargon: passer takes être for passing by ('nous sommes passés') but avoir for spending time (j'ai passé une semaine).

target: Ils sont morts dans un accident de voiture.
english: They died in a car accident.
old: Mourir uses être: ils sont morts. This is part of the DR MRS VANDERTRAMP verbs.
focus: 'Ils sont morts' looks like 'they are dead' but it is passe compose 'they died' - mourir takes etre; cut the VANDERTRAMP mnemonic

target: Elle travaillait dans une librairie à cette époque.
english: She worked in a bookstore at that time.
old: 'À cette époque' (at that time) sets a past context for describing how things were.
focus: name the payoff - 'a cette epoque' is a signal to choose imparfait (travaillait); say the tense outright instead of 'sets a past context'

target: Ils devaient prendre le train de sept heures.
english: They had to take the seven o'clock train.
old: Devoir in imparfait expresses past obligation or necessity: ils devaient = they had to.
focus: ils devaient = were supposed to / had to with the outcome left open - contrast ils ont du (had to and did); not just 'devaient = they had to'

target: Nous sommes allés à la plage le week-end dernier.
english: We went to the beach last weekend.
old: Motion/state-change verbs (`aller`, `venir`, `partir`, `mourir`, `naître`, all reflexives) take `être`. The rest take `avoir`.
focus: strip backticks; anchor in this card's 'nous sommes alles' - motion/state-change verbs take etre, the rest avoir

target: Il pleuvait depuis deux heures quand le soleil est apparu.
english: It had been raining for two hours when the sun appeared.
old: Imparfait + depuis expresses duration in the past. PC marks when the situation changed.
focus: English 'had been raining' = plain imparfait + depuis in French (il pleuvait depuis deux heures); spell out passe compose, no 'PC' abbreviation

target: J'ai eu envie de partir en voyagé.
english: I felt like taking a trip.
old: Avoir envie de = to feel like or to want to. Past: j'ai eu envie de.
focus: avoir envie de = to feel like, NOT envy - French 'has' the urge; hook the false friend and quote j'ai eu envie

target: Nous avions l'habitude de dîner à vingt heures.
english: We used to have dinner at eight PM.
old: Avoir l'habitude de + infinitive = to be in the habit of. Imparfait for past habits.
focus: one rule only - avoir l'habitude de = 'used to', literally 'had the habit of'; cut the generic imparfait-habits second sentence

target: Il pouvait courir très vite à cette époque.
english: He used to be able to run very fast at that time.
old: Pouvoir in imparfait describes a past ability or possibility: il pouvait = he could.
focus: il pouvait = ongoing past ability; sharpen with the classic contrast il a pu = managed to (one occasion), quoting pouvait courir

target: Tu avais faim quand tu es rentré du travail ?
english: Were you hungry when you came home from work?
old: States and feelings use imparfait (avais faim). Completed actions use PC (es rentre).
focus: states and feelings take imparfait (avais faim) vs the completed event (es rentré) – spell out passé composé, fix the missing accents

target: Tu avais dix ans quand tu as déménagé en France ?
english: Were you ten years old when you moved to France?
old: Age in the past uses imparfait (avais). Moving is a completed event: PC (as demenage).
focus: age in the past is always imparfait (tu avais dix ans); the move is the event (as déménagé) – expand the PC abbreviation, fix accents

target: Elle faisait la cuisine quand elle s'est coupé le doigt.
english: She was cooking when she cut her finger.
old: Reflexive verbs in PC: elle s'est coupé. Imparfait for the background action.
focus: the gem is no agreement on s'est coupé because le doigt is the direct object (body-part rule) – drop the imparfait aside, one rule only

target: Je me suis trompé de route.
english: I took the wrong road.
old: Se tromper = to make a mistake. Je me suis trompé: agreement with masculine subject.
focus: se tromper de + noun = get the wrong one (trompé de route = took the wrong road) – lead with the idiom, cut the agreement aside

target: Il pleuvait quand nous sommes sortis.
english: It was raining when we went out.
old: Background weather (imparfait) vs completed action (passé composé).
focus: anchor in this card: il pleuvait is the weather backdrop, nous sommes sortis the event – quote both, keep it one line

target: Tu te souviens de notre première rencontre ?
english: Do you remember our first meeting?
old: Se souvenir de = to remember. The reflexive pronoun is essential for meaning.
focus: remembering is reflexive in French and drags de along: tu te souviens de – hook on the English mismatch, cut the vague 'essential for meaning'

target: Il faut que l'on prenne le train de six heures.
english: We need to take the six o'clock train.
old: After expressions of will/necessity/emotion + `que`, French switches to subjunctive. `Je veux que tu viennes` (not viens) = 'I want you to come'.
focus: il faut que flips the verb to subjunctive: prenne, not prend – quote this card, strip backticks and the off-card viennes example

target: Nous cherchons un hôtel qui ait une piscine.
english: We're looking for a hotel that has a pool.
old: Subjunctive in relative clauses when the antecedent is not yet identified or uncertain.
focus: ait, not a: the hotel is still hypothetical (being searched for) – drop 'antecedent'/'relative clause' jargon, quote qui ait une piscine

target: Il faut que tout le monde soit prêt à huit heures.
english: Everyone needs to be ready at eight o'clock.
old: After expressions of will/necessity/emotion + `que`, French switches to subjunctive. `Je veux que tu viennes` (not viens) = 'I want you to come'.
focus: second telling, different angle from fr-1598: être goes irregular in subjunctive – il faut que ... soit, not est; strip backticks

target: Je ne le sais pas.
english: I don't know it.
old: In negation, the pronoun stays before the verb: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.
focus: the pronoun sits inside the ne...pas sandwich: Je ne le sais pas – quote this card's own words
